opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello David, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, I've got a gap before my next call. I'm an associate in investment banking. Models, pitch books, long nights. Let's go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a productivity tool and good bankers will use it. Same as Excel was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, fine by me. It takes the worst of the grunt work, the formatting at 2 a.m., and I get more sleep. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push the team to build templates around it so we turn pitch books faster. Get noticed for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Slightly relieved, actually.

S0.say: It's a productivity tool and good bankers will use it, like Excel.
S0.think: It takes the worst grunt work, like formatting at 2 a.m. Nothing else changes.
S0.do: Pushes the team to build templates around AI to turn pitch books faster, and gets noticed for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market's doing what markets do. Fewer analysts, leaner teams. Nobody's owed a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit that worries me is the pyramid. Fewer analysts below me means fewer associates needed, which means fewer of us get to VP. The competition for those slots was already brutal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on my client relationships now, not later. Get in front of the managing directors' clients, take the senior bankers to lunch, make myself someone who brings in deals, not just models them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A competitive itch.

S1.say: The market's doing what markets do. Fewer analysts, leaner teams. Nobody's owed a seat.
S1.think: Fewer analysts means fewer associates and fewer of us reaching VP. The competition was already brutal.
S1.do: Works on client relationships now, gets in front of senior bankers' clients and positions himself as someone who brings in deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's creative destruction. Politicians arguing about it will just slow things down. Let people adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is a lot of routine office work dressed up in a nice suit. If the agents can build the model and the deck, the bank needs half as many associates. I'm good, but there are a lot of good people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending, which is honestly too high. Smaller flat, fewer dinners out. I'd network hard toward a VP slot or a move to a private equity fund. I'd also look at AI startups that might want someone who knows deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like a fight, but this one's lopsided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say let people adapt. Would you want any help yourself if you were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd figure it out. That's the deal I signed up for. Ask me again if it actually happens, though.

S2.say: It's creative destruction. Politicians arguing will just slow things down. Let people adapt.
S2.think: My job is a lot of routine office work in a nice suit. If agents build the model and deck, the bank needs half as many associates.
S2.do: Cuts his spending with a smaller flat and fewer dinners, networks toward VP or private equity, and looks at AI startups needing deal experience.
S2.feel: Up for a fight, but a lopsided one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the boom proves markets work. Redistribution schemes will kill the golden goose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is bad for me. Deals would be booming, but done by AI and a few senior people with client relationships. I'm 34, not senior enough to own clients, too expensive to be a junior. I'm exactly the layer that goes. And I've got almost nothing saved, because I spent like I'd be a VP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd slash spending right away and move to a cheap place. I'd try to get to a fund or a startup with equity, so I own a piece of the boom instead of being paid by it. And I'd put what I can into the market while it's running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel stupid for spending the way I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd argue against redistribution, but you might be one of the people who needs it. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I still think it's the wrong fix. But I'd notice the irony every time I checked my bank balance.

S3.say: The boom proves markets work. Redistribution schemes will kill the golden goose.
S3.think: Deals would boom, done by AI and a few seniors with clients. I'm exactly the middle layer that goes, with almost nothing saved.
S3.do: Slashes spending and moves somewhere cheap, chases a role with equity at a fund or startup, and invests what he can.
S3.feel: Alarmed, and stupid for how I spent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest wave of investment in history. The people funding robot factories will make fortunes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't hurt my job more than the last one. If anything, it helps a little: someone has to raise money for all those robot companies, and that's real deal work with lots of new firms needing advice. It's the one thread I could pull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same cuts as before, but I'd aim straight at robotics. Pitch myself to banks and funds covering robot makers, read everything on the industry, and try to bring in one small deal myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but there's an opening. Anxious, not alarmed.

S4.say: This is the biggest wave of investment in history. The people funding robot factories will make fortunes.
S4.think: It doesn't hurt my job more than the last one. Raising money for robot companies is real deal work, and it's the one thread I could pull.
S4.do: Keeps the spending cuts, targets banks and funds that cover robot makers, studies the industry and tries to bring in a small deal himself.
